column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Eyewitness accounts are partial: in Vansina's own collection of about a thousand Libyan-war accounts, almost no informant could see a whole battle; memory fills gaps from expectation and the logic of 'what must have happened'. Use in the oral lesson: test every eyewitness claim for what the witness could see.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Hypercritical rejection is wrong in practice: if all perception were so uncertain nobody could act on memory, so eyewitness accounts should be scrutinised, not discarded. Use as the balance point in the oral-tradition lesson.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Hearsay is the fountainhead of most tradition: rumours that are not contradicted survive and become oral history, then oral tradition; a tradition built on rumour tells more about the mentality of the time than about the events. Use in the oral lesson on what a tradition can prove.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Nongqause's prophecy of 1856 told the Xhosa to kill their cattle for the return of the ancestors; it is remembered for its consequences, since the famine that followed broke Xhosa resistance to European pressure. Use in the frontier and Shaka lessons: a prophecy is evidence of its effects.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: King Dingiswayo's dream of bringing peace through universal conquest is said to legitimise, after the fact, the Zulu (Natal) imperialism of his age. Use in the Shaka lesson: a dream recorded later can justify a state's expansion.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Reminiscences are organised self-portraits: informants forget what is inconvenient and reshape the rest, and many cultures keep a public mask apart from a private face. Use in the oral-history lesson when a life story is the source.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Rossini's anecdote about meeting Beethoven grew into a tale over the years after the first telling; use it as a warning that retold stories gain episodes. Use in the oral lesson on growth of stories over time.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Iconatrophy: explanations given for monuments and natural features (hand prints of heroes, the legend of Pope Joan from a statue) are spurious explanations made after the fact, so stories tied to sites need caution and cannot be rejected or accepted wholesale. Use in the lesson on oral traditions about places.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Popular etymologies are seldom innocent: the Kinshasa place name Kalina belongs to an Austro-Hungarian officer who drowned there in 1884 but became a genealogical claim by 1957; the Baule ethnonym is explained as 'they threw' with a sacrifice tale. Use in the Guinea coast and Akan lessons on names and origin tales.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Explanatory glosses on obscure sayings can date to the events but be altered: the Rundi saying 'It is cracking at Nkoondo' refers to a late nineteenth-century battle, but other versions name different parties. Use in the lesson on oral sayings as sources.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Speculative genealogies give origins for cultures (Tetela brothers as ancestors of the Luba and Kuba); Baumann's view is that such tales are excellent sources for cultural history, though they may preserve archaic features. Use in the lesson on origin genealogies.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 1, Oral Tradition as Process)
column5: Verbal art: dirges use stock images, a poet may compose deliberately for hours (a Rwandan poet, the author saw), and tales develop in performance from older bits, so a tale has no single date and is hard to date. Use in the lesson on oral literature as evidence.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: Memorised speech (prayers, formulas, poems) is the one class where archetypes can be reconstructed by comparing versions; tales and some epics have no original to recover. Use in the oral lesson: say which kind of tradition is being used before comparing versions.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: A Mbuun rain-chasing spell keeps names from a migration period and a quarrel with the Samba; its core has stayed stable because it wishes rain on people who have not been neighbours for centuries. Use in the oral lesson: a stable core can survive centuries even when wording changes.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: A Denkyira dirge (Ntim Gyakari, the last king, who lost his kingdom to Asante at Feyiase in 1701) is a source only with its commentary: the poem names the battle, and the date comes from the story around it. Use in the Akan lesson on dirges as evidence of the Asante rise.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: An Oromo poem sung in jail after the 1876 conquest of the poet's land by Menelik's general Goobana is understood only with commentary. Use in the Ethiopia lesson as the example of a poem whose date comes from its context.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: Historical gossip can be very long-lived: a caravan guide's story in 1954 of the 'sun-fire people' matched a tale told by Herodotus and Pliny some 2,500 years earlier. Use in the oral lesson: a long-lived story is not thereby true, and the match must be explained.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: The Hopi ambush case (1853 to 1856) gives three versions: the bare facts in 1892, a survivor's reminiscence three weeks later, and a 1936 published version in which the event becomes predestined, with a clan's charter on the boundary. Use as the worked example of how a tradition changes from memory to charter.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: Group accounts end as clichés: a claim that all Upper Nile migrations were caused by a quarrel between brothers over a trifle shows how one stock story can replace many accounts. Use in the migration lessons as a warning against stock explanations.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: Borrowed motifs in origin traditions: the Tower of Babel motif explains population differences across Africa, and the first Burundi king is in some versions a sheepherder who overcame a false king. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on origin stories.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: The Kuba added the sea to their migration origin after hearing of the ocean from Imbangala traders, giving tides and waves to the cradle point; the last stages of the migration reflect where the chiefs' capitals stood. Use in the Congo basin lesson as an example of later detail added to an origin.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes)
column5: Traditions of origin are logical constructs and cosmologies, often genealogical; migration stories are cosmologies too, and whole bodies of accounts can collapse into one culture hero. Use in the oral lesson on origin traditions.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: The floating gap: a tradition's time-reckoning reaches only so far (for the Aka of Lobaye, about one generation of adults); beyond it accounts fuse into a culture hero or are forgotten. For the Tio, the 1880 arrival of de Brazza would by 1960 have moved into the period of origins. Use in the oral lesson on time depth.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: A body of oral accounts typically has three tiers: recent times, which thin out going back; a floating gap with one or a few names; and a period of origins with rich material. Use in the oral lesson as the shape to expect.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Cumulative accounts (genealogies, king lists) are kept up to date because they justify present relationships and office, and lists need mnemonic devices to survive; so they are manipulated. Use in the dates lesson on genealogies and king lists.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: The Jaziya epic, told from Jordan to Algeria, refers to the Banu Hilal invasion of Tunisia in 1049-53 and was mentioned by Ibn Khaldun shortly after 1400; epics may last longer than poems. Use in the Hilali migration lesson as an oral source for the invasion.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Tales have no original and no fixed composition; their material is of mixed age, so in non-literate societies tale material is dated to the latest possible date, often the later nineteenth century. Use in the oral lesson on tales as evidence.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Historical tales in Rwanda: a cycle of popular tales about King Ruganzu Ndori mixes in other tales and gives the 'there once was a king' type the name Ruganzu, so the popular version shows artistic licence beside the historical accounts. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on royal tales.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Famous last words are mostly apocryphal but sum up a career, such as Andriampoinimerina's saying that the ocean is the border of his ricefield, which set a programme for his heir to conquer Madagascar. Use in the Madagascar lesson on how later generations summed up a ruler.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Definition: an oral tradition is a verbal statement about the past, spoken or sung, transmitted by word of mouth over more than one generation; sources for oral history (the living memory of informants) are a different class. Use as the working definition at the start of the oral lesson.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Vansina's view against Miller's: traditions need not be cliches or narratives, and oral sources that are not about the past can testify despite themselves, which makes them more reliable. Use in the oral lesson on how to read non-historical testimony.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Transmission is communal, not a neat chain: news passes through many people and fuses in the telling, yet a link must still exist between observation and record for the message to be evidence; a tradition is a series of lost documents, evidence at second or nth remove. Use in the oral lesson on the chain of transmission.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Mixed transmission: once a tradition is written it can feed back into oral tradition, and this mixed period can last long, as in Madagascar; historians should trace whether a tradition has been recorded several times. Use in the Madagascar lesson on written and oral traditions.

column4: ch-005.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 1, Dynamic Processes and Definition)
column5: Statements about situations or trends (funeral etiquette, bridewealth inflation) often generalise norms and opinions rather than observed events; they testify to mentalities. Tales give evidence about situations. Use in the oral lesson: say whether a claim reports an event or a norm.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: A tale is never just a recitation: teller and audience create it together, the teller reads the audience and expands or condenses; every performance is new but presupposes an old tale. Use in the oral lesson on what a performance is.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Rwandan historical accounts (ibiteekerezo) could run a whole evening, performed quietly for a lord and his guests, while Burundi accounts were short, told in turn over beer. The form of performance shapes the account. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on how Rwandan and Burundian traditions were told.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Record the performer, place and date of a performance: Frobenius's 1906 Kuba tale of the dwarf antelope killed by the leopard, told by a Lulua slave, makes sense only as defiance, because the dwarf antelope is the trickster hero. Use in the source-criticism lesson: the teller can change a tale's meaning.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Specialists differ: griots and court historians hold office, Rwandan abiiru keep ritual rather than memorise history, and the Ketu baba elegun was rewarded for a flawless recital; Kagame's picture of Rwandan archivists is overdrawn. Use in the oral lesson on who the teller is.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Kuba royal history: a king could not be interrupted, and the sanctions for a wrong recital were fictive; control came from public consensus, yet the requirement encouraged mastery. Use in the Congo basin lesson on how a court kept its history.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Encyclopaedic informants: among the Kuba, Bope Louis was an antiquarian of historical slogans and Shep Mathias built a grand design of the past; collectors must say whether a recital came from such a person. Use in the oral lesson on informants.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Frequency of performance and fidelity do not match: Dogon Sigui rituals were performed once in sixty years, and tales told many nights a month change faster than rare ones. Use in the oral lesson on what keeps a text stable.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 2, Performance)
column5: Fidelity comes from sanctions or competition, not from the medium alone: Hawaiian chants of 618 lines match across islands, Rwandan controllers could face death for error, and rival poets were rewarded, so the poems hardly vary. Use in the oral lesson on memorised texts.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Memory works by cueing and scanning: each item is labelled with a cue, often coded twice (auditory and visual), and tales hang on a core image with a short cliché as its cue. Use in the oral lesson on how a memorised tradition is held.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Mnemonic objects can record more than a fact: the Inca quipu of knotted cords read as a record of each king's reign length and conduct; Sioux winter counts and Iroquois pegged canes were cues to events and chiefs' lists. Use in the written-sources lesson: objects and knots were records before writing, not merely decoration.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Landscape is a mnemonic: tomb sites, battlefields and the tee grounds of the Mae Enga keep history in place, and a Shilluk monarch is said to have built a false tomb to support a traditional history. Use in the evidence lesson: a site can be read as a record, and a fake record can be built.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Drum slogans and drum names in West African kingdoms, and tonal melodies, preserve historical information; in Rwanda dynastic poets learned the melody first and the words to fit it. Use in the Ghana and Mali lessons on drums and praise songs as sources.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Learning is mostly by imitation and attendance: Tikopia traditions were learned during breaks in kava rites with controllers present; a Marquesan father hired a bard and a school of about thirty pupils for a month of taboo instruction. Use in the oral lesson on how a tradition passes to its next holder.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Rwandan dynastic poem (ukwibyara): six performances give 396 to 441 verses in the full versions and a 277-verse fragment, with small verse variants, omissions, and two kings both called Mibambwe confused; the variants can be ordered into a genealogy, so an archetype can be reconstructed. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on how far a court poem can be trusted.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Kuba clan slogans vary by choice of discourse, not by copying error: rain slogans link the Ndoong, Bieng and Kweemy clans, so a stemma codicum of written texts falsifies oral variation. Use in the oral lesson: a stemma works for copies, not for performed set speech.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 2, Mnemonic devices and variability)
column5: Epic versions differ: Lord's comparison of the Alija Stocevic song (1935 and 1950 performances) shows omissions and changes of detail, and no original exists to reconstruct. Use in the oral lesson on epic as a source.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Variation in epic (Central African Mwindo, Balkan singers): plots and episodes change with many performers over time, and the historian must separate the general epic corpus from one epic's plot. Use in the oral lesson on epic.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Historical accounts vary far less than epic or set speech: two Rwandan versions of one story told by Gakaniisha in 1952 and 1957 differed less than the Stocevic epic versions, and a tradition that crystallises within a generation is close to its first telling. Use in the oral lesson on the time span of a tradition.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Authenticity: Ossian's poems were invented by Macpherson, not based on any performance; the Walam Olum of the Delaware, published by Raffinesque in 1833 from sticks and songs he said he had received, is likely a forgery or a revival. Use in the source-criticism lesson on claimed traditions.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Authorship: every performer of an unmemorised genre is an author; ask whether the recorded performer was a professional, a man of memory, and from whom he learned, because that can be checked against other living people. Use in the oral lesson on informants.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Ukwibyara, the Rwandan dynastic poem, was composed by Nyakayonga about the middle of the nineteenth century, and his descendants' genealogy correlates with the recorded versions; the Ndoong slogan can be dated only to its recording (1953). Use in the Great Lakes lesson: only the recording date is usually known for a tradition.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Incidental mention: Einhard's Life of Charlemagne (about 830) names Roland in an ambush also in the Royal Annals, but other sources omit him and the name may be a later insertion; the 'according to oral tradition' summaries are too far from a performance to carry an argument. Use in the source-criticism lesson on stray mentions.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Systematic official traditions: the Japanese Ko-jiki (about 712) came from an imperial search, selection, removal of 'untruths' and conflation of many accounts; Njoya's history of Bamum was built from many performances by its king. Use in the oral lesson: say whether a history was selected, approved or harvested.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: Recording conditions bias the result: Libyan war veterans had benefit claims, so some who had not fought posed as veterans; a young collector was steered by a few leaders and heard only one side of a dispute. Use in the oral lesson on sampling and the informant's motive.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 2, Variability, authenticity and recording)
column5: An interview has two authors; leading questions reduce the informant's voice; group interviews give only what all agree on; compromises between informants are invented on the spot (the Bokila claim to be first). Use in the oral lesson on interview method and why confrontation fails.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 2, Testimony and text)
column5: A testimony is a tradition as actualised by one person: the same informant can give two contradictory stories and each is a separate testimony; a single informant's lists before and after asking an uncle are two testimonies. Use in the oral lesson: name the informant and the conditions, not just 'the tradition'.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 2, Testimony and text)
column5: Rwanda 1958-60: informants told two origin stories for the Tutsi and Hutu (brothers from Kanyarwanda's sons, or Kigwa the first Tutsi falling from the sky) and never combined them, choosing one as true; both were legitimations in a brewing civil war. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on origin stories and politics.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 2, Testimony and text)
column5: Text versus testimony: several oral renderings are one text in several versions, and fusing them into a reconstructed original is a mistake; Gakaniisha's 1954 and 1957 accounts are one text with the second shorter because the researcher already knew the story. Use in the oral lesson on editing oral texts.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 2, Testimony and text)
column5: Interviews are social processes: informants volunteer information only after months, when they know the interviewer; a questionnaire yields minimal and often inaccurate answers given under duress. Use in the oral lesson on fieldwork.

column4: ch-006.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 2, Testimony and text)
column5: A recording session is not a live performance: the Kuba king recited official traditions in 1953 before his court outside his coronation, and the record loses gesture, audience reaction and sound once published. Use in the oral lesson: say whether a text is a performance or a session.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Jousse's claim that all oral literature obeys syntactic laws is not convincing; the real difference from written texts is more repetition, because oral messages need redundancy and a written text can be re-read. Use in the oral lesson on what marks oral form.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Performers often do not know the rules they follow: the Somali gabay has metre and alliteration that poets do not name, so only linguistic analysis finds tonal rhyme and parallelism. Use in the oral lesson: ask a linguist, not only the informant, about form.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Fillers in epic (the phrase 'that white city' in a Serbian line) are formulas for the metre and must not be read as meaning; compare versions to separate intended from apparent meaning. Use in the oral lesson on reading an epic line.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Form governs stability: a Rundi praise song with a rigid two-part structure was never found in another version, while Serbo-Croat poetry varies because formulas are easily exchanged. Use in the oral lesson: predict variation from the form.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Worked example of narrative structure: the Kurumba account of the origin of the Ganame chieftaincy has episodes, a plot, and two core images (conception through eating and magic war at the village pond); the chapter uses it to separate plot, episode, setting and theme. Use in the oral lesson as the model for reading an account.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Tension in tales depends on how many outcomes an episode leaves open; an episode with one outcome kills interest. Use in the oral lesson on tales as performance, not as record.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Rule of thumb: the more artistic a narrative, the less it probably reflects a sequence of events; but a brilliant denouement can still be true (a rebel executed just as his pardon came), and the claim must be tested against many versions. Use in the source-criticism lesson.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 3, Form and content)
column5: Genre decides change: setting and personages may change between versions of a tale, but must not change in a narrative of events believed to have happened, which is what separates a tale from an account. Use in the oral lesson on genre.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: Genres are named locally and defined by form and content together: the Kuba shoosh slogans look like songs and proverbs to an outsider, so the local name and its rules decide the genre. Use in the oral lesson: list genres by local name before comparing traditions.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: No universal genre classification works: a 'praise poem' category lumps Kuba slogans with Rwandan dynastic poems, and a European fable and an Indian etiological tale fall into different classes. Use in the oral lesson: genre schemes from one culture do not travel.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: For historians the key genre question is whether a genre is taken as true or as fiction: Russian skazki may vary at will while byliny claim to tell what really happened, so Propp's morphology fits tales but not byliny. Use in the source-criticism lesson on claimed truth.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: The historian works with a text, a mutilated performance: tone, body language and the audience's response are lost, so apparent meaning and intended meaning must be separated. Use in the oral lesson on reading a transcript.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: Language limits the collector: a historian of the Ijo of the Niger Delta published with a linguist who knew the language, and any interpreted or translated testimony needs answers about the interpreter, the tapes and the collector's command. Use in the oral lesson on language and translation.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: Key words carry whole worldviews (Kongo nkisi, Luba buloji, Malagasy hasina) and have no literal translation, so a translated testimony can lose its meaning at the key word. Use in the oral lesson on translation.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: Archaic shouts can lose their meaning in the community yet keep a use: the Kuba shout 'nee boola' has a meaning in Mongo, but to the Kuba it signals 'we follow you'. Use in the oral lesson: check meaning in the situation of performance.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: The Oromo song about the elephant's hair (duuri, xuuri) is said to be Jote's reason for not campaigning against a neighbour who was his brother-in-law; the lines carry an intended meaning that the words alone do not give. Use in the oral lesson on intended meaning.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 3, Genre and meaning)
column5: Rwandan dynastic poems allude instead of naming: Kiganda alludes to the death of King Ndahiro, and kings are named by capitals or other places, so the allusion must be explained before the history can be used. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on how Rwandan poetry names kings.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 3, Stereotypes and aims)
column5: Numbers are stereotypes: four is perfection in parts of West Africa, nine among the Kuba, four among the Maya, and 144 means infinity in Yoruba; the same number may mean the number or perfection. Use in the oral lesson on reading numbers in tradition.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 3, Stereotypes and aims)
column5: A cliché travels: a chief's trap under a mat, the subordinate who dances into the pit or probes with a spear, is told as history from the Yaka of the Kwango to the Luapula people and the Kuba, each time as if it happened to them. Use in the Congo basin lesson on shared stories.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 3, Stereotypes and aims)
column5: Intended testimony differs from intended meaning: a tale is meant to amuse, and the detail that slaves traded redwood blocks to buy their freedom was incidental, unintended, and so trustworthy. Use in the oral lesson: prize what a source did not mean to say.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 3, Stereotypes and aims)
column5: Royal lists are performed to prove the present king's right and kingship's normal order; the historical aim is secondary, shown by the solemn occasions of recitation (coronations, burials). Use in the king-list lessons: ask what a list was for.

column4: ch-007.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 3, Stereotypes and aims)
column5: Many historians of oral societies collect only intended narratives, yet unintentional material is often the most trustworthy and is usually found by those who study a community's verbal arts over time. Use in the oral lesson on what to collect.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Messages are social products with a social surface: they are told because they matter to the community, and a claim that oral tradition holds no message from the past goes too far, because cultural continuities need explaining. Use as the opening note of the oral lesson on social context.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Performance occasions decide the form a record takes: Kuba royal history is told as anecdotes, and a formal succession framework only at coronations, so a coherent 'annals' misjudged the kingdom's history; genealogies are rarely performed whole. Use in the king-list lessons: check the occasion before reading a list as a chronicle.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Haphazard talk carries about two generations of lore in daily channels, and speculation can harden into tradition: 'it could have been' becomes 'it was'. Use in the oral lesson on how commentary becomes record.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Secret histories: the Inca state chose which history could be popularised and kept the quipu keepers' data closed; Vansina reads the selection as justifying the regime as it was. Use in the oral lesson on state control of the past.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Akan official history says the ruling dynasties are indigenous, though royal clans know some secret versions make them immigrants; transmission of traditions contradicting the official version was forbidden. Use in the Akan lesson on official and secret royal history.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Official and private are relative: one group's official history is private about others, and official traditions give a wider frame in time and space but mainly the elite's view. Use in the oral lesson on whose history a source gives.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Traditions as weapons: among the Nzebi a palaver on clan history can decide social relations (a founder who 'acquired a following by the harp' means slave origin); among the Kongo, elders manipulated genealogies to deny land rights to others. Use in the Congo basin lesson on genealogies as power.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: In Burundi there were no general official historical accounts, only short installation songs, so the foundation accounts are private at the national level and official only for local ritual groups. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on what counted as official history.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 4, Social uses)
column5: Functions are shown by use: a royal genealogy legitimises monarchy, the family's right to office and the present king; the claim is confirmed when it is recited at accession or argued in court, and contradictory versions of a tribute collector reveal the point of each village's claim. Use in the oral lesson on function and use.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: A saint's legend in north-west Tunisia (Sidi Mhammad, the herdsman whose shrine outranks Sidi Slima's) legitimises the precedence of the Arfawa over their hosts, the same function that genealogies serve; its use exposes it to suspicion of distortion. Use in the Maghrib Islam lesson on saint traditions.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: King lists were falsified: Rwanda's king Rwaaka was dropped from the official list after his brother overcame him; the Imbangala list is short because only formally installed kings were recorded, a problem also for Loango and recent Tio rulers. Use in the Kongo and Angola lesson on king lists.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: Tradition builds group identity: the Ngoni of Malawi stress every difference from their neighbours to keep their nationhood when assimilation threatened, and the Lumbee of North Carolina claimed an origin that won them recognition as Indians. Use in the Ngoni lesson on identity and origin stories.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: Idealisation: a Kuba king was an ideal tyrant fifty years after his death; anecdotes move to prototypes (the magician, the warrior, the culture hero), so a tradition's corpus models how society should work and is only occasionally a record. Use in the oral lesson on ideal types.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: Whose past is history? In Kazembe and other kingdoms the dynasty's past was the nation's past, so descent groups' stories feature kings; in small societies the big man replaces the court as the point of reference. Use in the Luapula and Lunda lessons on court-centred history.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: Test for idealisation: traits and anecdotes that run counter to a tradition's purpose are the most reliable, such as official accounts of kings killed by enemies and an emblem lost in war (Rwanda), while other data need discussion, not automatic acceptance. Use in the oral lesson on checking a tradition.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: Performers have interests: a Rwandan poem's author warned the king against a rival's duplicity, and the reason is known only because a separate story survives; Kuba bulaam add speculation to show expertise and Tonga experts guard knowledge. Use in the oral lesson on the performer's motive.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 4, Justifications and idealisation)
column5: Recording changes the informant: by the 1950s Lulua told a school version of their origin (Nsangu Lubangu) that the old men rejected, and informants judge the fieldworker's label and motives; a Kuba suspicion of witchcraft shows how a collector can be misread. Use in the oral lesson on schools and fieldwork.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: Burundi and Rwanda compare sharply: Rwanda's centralised bureaucracy and royal genealogies produced dynastic poetry and many genres, while Burundi's collectively ruling abaganwa and shifting provinces left no official historians and little historical memory. Use in the Great Lakes lesson to explain why the two kingdoms' traditions differ.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: Structural time depth: the Tio recognise only two generations back, so an earlier migration is told as the grandfather's event, while the Lunda's structural depth of four generations leads straight to mythical founders; a tradition's time depth is what its society can count. Use in the oral lesson on time depth and in the dates lesson.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: Significance decides what is remembered: the Assiniboine adopted the horse in the eighteenth century, yet their traditions say horses existed since creation, while the Nez Perce kept a tradition of the horse's introduction that shows less change. Use in the oral lesson on why an important event can vanish.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: Kuba memory of Europeans kept the first merchant and dropped the second, who took the country for the Congo Free State, because the second was no longer a novelty. Use in the Congo basin lesson on the colonial arrival.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: The repertory of intentional historical accounts is small (origins, migrations, descent, war, catastrophe) and coheres as a blueprint of the political system, as Oliver shows for the Merina: the corpus shows how the kingdom should work, not only how it did. Use in the Madagascar lesson on the Merina repertory.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: Goody's homeostasis claim (traditions always match society) is an overstatement: Firth found no link between a Tikopia group's prestigious origin claim and its rank, and Kuba dynastic tradition keeps traces of irregular succession, which suggests that irregular succession was the norm. Use in the oral lesson on congruence and in the king-list lessons.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: Kuba dynastic tradition tends to suppress irregular successions, yet traces remain so that irregular succession was the norm; use this in the Kuba king-list lesson. Use in the Congo basin lesson on what official lists leave out.

column4: ch-008.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 4, Tradition mirrors society)
column5: The historian can check distortion, but only in part: suspicious congruences show where a tradition was altered, and the imprint of the present can be assessed through fieldwork and through the time the data were recorded. Use as the closing rule of the oral lesson on social distortion.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: Culture is what is common in a group's minds: Goody overstates the uniformity of oral societies and understates the standardising of reading publics, and in both kinds of society idiosyncrasy and interest remain. Use in the oral lesson on what a shared tradition assumes.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: Kuba space: rivers organise direction into upstream and downstream, and the world began at the sacred downstream point, so migrations are told as going upstream from there to the sea; right is superior to left, both defined facing a river's source. Use in the Congo basin lesson on how migration stories encode space.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: Time is a single concept of duration in which linear and cyclical time coexist (Bali; Ainu waves of creation); the claim that Africans had three separate times, timeless, cyclical and linear, does not hold on closer inspection. Use in the oral lesson on time concepts.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: Historical truth is culture-specific: Chamula truth is a coherent account retold and certified by ancestors; Trobriand truth needs a trace in the landscape to be factual; Rundi accept even a Kingdom of Women as real. Use in the source-criticism lesson: ask what truth means in the source's own culture.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: In Mande land the truthfulness of a speaker depends on the antiquity of his professional family, so the griot's word carries weight by lineage. Use in the Mali lesson on griots and truth.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: Kuba truth is guaranteed by the councils: the kuum rehearses in secret before a spokesman speaks, and an old chief said what was once true is now false and the reverse; a deed is accepted because witnesses and councils certify it. Use in the Congo basin lesson on how a court validates its history.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 5, Culture and basic concepts)
column5: Causality in oral societies is appearance: institutions appear fully formed under a named king or culture hero, history is a sequence of steady states, and each invention is added by a leader rather than changed; this explains why tradition is told as anecdotes about king A or B. Use in the oral lesson and in the states lessons on how African kings are presented.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: Kuba origin accounts: the Kuba told of a sea shore with waves and whites in armour, but these details were taken over as revelation; when the Imbangala arrived in the eighteenth century they confirmed the belief that origins lay at the most downstream point, so the detail was added. Use in the Congo basin lesson: a visitor's arrival can confirm and so enlarge an origin story.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: Feierman's reading of the Mbegha cliché (the outcast hunter who founds the Shambaa kingdom in Tanzania) parallels a rite of passage and sets hunter against farmer, masculine against feminine; it is replicable because each step has Shambaa support, but the kingdom dates only from the eighteenth century while the imagery is older. Use in the East African interior lesson on Shambaa origins.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: A worldview must be elicited by asking, and caution is needed with etiological tales: the lion is a symbol of kingship except where Tio kings were held to command lions; a symbol is not the same as a reality. Use in the oral lesson on symbol and reality.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: Images carry emotional resonance, and an interpretation must show that the audience feels it: in Rwanda the verb for a bull's lowing, used of kings, recalls cult mediums and fertility, and the claim needs direct evidence of audience response. Use in the oral lesson on images and the risk of overinterpretation.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: In Rwanda and Burundi kings' utterances were described with the verb for a bull's lowing, which recalls the Kiranga cult; the resonance of authority and manhood is sustained in the audience. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on royal speech.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: A cliché is a deliberate, compressed simplification that must be read symbolically; signs that it is not literal include breaches of natural law and repetition in the corpus, and Firth's Tikopia incidents needed reinterpretation with no agreed principles. Use in the oral lesson on reading stock stories.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: Explicit, intended and implicit meaning are different: an interpreter's reading is only a discovered meaning unless it can be shown to be what the makers intended; Miller's reading of communal charms as successive political regimes (lunga before ngola) claims implicit meaning and must be demonstrated. Use in the oral lesson on contested readings of traditions.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 5, Worldview, images and cliches)
column5: The Imbangala king's name, Kinguri, is also the title of his office, so an account of his death may mean the abolition of kingship; there is no way to decide whether the tradition is symbolic. Use in the Congo basin lesson on names that are also titles.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 5, Guidelines for implicit meaning)
column5: Guidelines for implicit meaning: compare the message with other versions to spot stereotypes; expand the core images and find the core plot; accept only imagery known in the culture; say how the tradition was probably altered; and do not assume one stereotype has one meaning, since images are multivocal. Use in the oral lesson as the step-by-step test for any cliché.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 5, Guidelines for implicit meaning)
column5: A Burundi claimant around 1900, Kilima, used the stereotype that a true heir was spirited away as a child and returned to claim the throne; the stereotype covers a conquest, and because many Rundi believed it the claimant could use it. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on royal succession stories.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 5, Guidelines for implicit meaning)
column5: Forces that alter messages: the Hopi account gained motivation, integration into a corpus of accounts, and aesthetic elaboration, driven by mnemonic dynamics. Use in the oral lesson on how a memory becomes a charter.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 5, Guidelines for implicit meaning)
column5: Do not decode explicit meaning at all costs: a stereotype's explicit meaning may be its intended meaning (no assumed hidden message), and an ambiguous cliché such as Kinguri may be best read literally. Use in the oral lesson as the caution against over-reading traditions.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Oral tradition is a pool of information in memory, not discrete documents: independent sources that agree can prove an event, but only if the sources really are independent, and a community's traditions are fused in common knowledge. Use in the oral lesson on independence of evidence.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: The Kuba court network: of 48 informants whose knowledge was recorded, 42 were linked to the royal court through teaching and borrowing, and written royal versions since 1885 fit the same network; the corpus is a social network, not a set of separate persons. Use in the Congo basin lesson on how Kuba knowledge is held.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Esoteric knowledge can be officially controlled yet widely known: among the Lovedu, the paternity of heirs was a secret punishable by death, yet clandestine genealogies circulated. Use in the southern African lesson on secret royal history.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: History as gossip is as important as performance in passing on the past; much information from writings or foreign oral sources fuses with local knowledge and cannot later be separated. Use in the oral lesson on the sources of what informants know.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Palimpsest: a charter myth for a ritual office (the title NaRhana in the Shi-Ngweshe region) contains older and newer layers, and Sigwalt traces the compromise stories to nineteenth-century political change; the older surviving portion still refers to an older situation. Use in the Congo basin lesson on how a title's story can be dated by its layers.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Local landmarks keep accounts alive: a mound at Mpiina Ntsa is one mound to outsiders but several with different persons to locals, and people near Burundi's royal capitals remember events of about 1900 better. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on sites and memory.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Diffusion explains most shared tales: the Kuba king's slogan is a translation of a Lulua slogan whose name it explains, and the pit hidden under a mat was not invented independently across the savanna kingdoms; motifs travel with their explanatory power. Use in the oral lesson on diffusion of traditions.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Noah's drunkenness was known to the Kuba and Lunda by the twentieth century, probably from Kongo mission teaching; the Imbangala borrowed the Lunda account of their first king Kinguri, which served their trade with the Lunda. Use in the Congo basin lesson on borrowed origins.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 6, The corpus as a pool)
column5: Henige: uncontaminated oral tradition hardly exists; written material feeds back into oral tradition and mixed transmission can last for centuries, so each written input must be checked. Use in the oral lesson on feedback from writing.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Interdependence: converging oral accounts are usually renderings of one tradition, not independent proofs (Delivre's rule; the synoptic Gospels as one oral milieu); oral evidence is 'on probation' until confirmed by writing, archaeology or linguistics and then serves as a research agenda. Use in the oral lesson: the test for independence before any claim is proven.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Rosaldo's convergent evidence and Thompson's mass collection work for recent, independent sources, but most oral history after the living elders' lifetimes cannot confirm itself; feedback and contamination are the norm. Use in the oral lesson on method.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Monuments and place names gain meaning by speculation that then passes for proof: Bigo's earthworks in Uganda were linked to the Cwezi by writers, and the Kuba depression explained as dancing after a king's installation was first an addition. Use in the oral lesson and the archaeology lessons on explanations fed back into the record.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Feedback in the Great Lakes: Rwandan and northern Burundian people called earlier sites the Renge, a name for the last population before the present one, and Bigo's link to a Cwezi kingdom came from writers whose speculation fed back into tradition. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on how sites and names are linked to dynasties.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Structuralist readings are not replicable or falsifiable: the Star Husband tale has been analysed seven times with seven results, and Lévi-Strauss's Asdiwal analysis misreports the ethnography; binary analysis is an association by the analyst. Use in the oral lesson as the caution against deep-structure readings.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Structure in Rwandan royal accounts: separate anecdotes about kings are ordered by reign and by a four-name cycle (one conquers, one is unlucky, one prospers, one is a legislator), attested in dynastic poetry of the eighteenth century at the latest; people reflect on the whole corpus without reciting it at once. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on how royal histories were ordered.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 6, Interdependence and structuring)
column5: Collective memory selects: Leach showed that a student remembers a succession by opposing pairs of figures (Henry VII and Elizabeth), so the whole corpus is organised by memory, not by a collective mind. Use in the oral lesson on how lists and successions are remembered.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 6, Structuring and chronology)
column5: Buganda's royal sequence (Kintu from the east, Cwa's false charge, Kalemera's exile, Kimera from the west, Tembo the rebel) is a structured cycle of founders and successors that ends with the first dynasty unrelated to the next and the land attacked from the west; Atkinson's reading is structuralist, and the principles of selection remain to be studied. Use in the Great Lakes lesson on Buganda's early kings, with the caution that the cycle is structured.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 6, Structuring and chronology)
column5: Structuring is recognised by patterns: a floating gap, founding heroes, epochs (reigns), and anecdotes grouped by topic; recent gossip is not structured, old material is; structuring slows after the first two generations, and the Hopi Spanish-arrival stories stopped changing about a generation after 1680. Use in the oral lesson on how to date structuring.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 6, Structuring and chronology)
column5: Effects of restructuring on history: temporal transposition, fusion of elements, discarded data and sequential reordering; but patterns in old accounts often rest on real key figures (founders as warriors, successors as organisers; the Tudor sequence), so they must be argued case by case and never used as the base of a major reconstruction. Use in the oral lesson on what structured tradition can prove.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 6, Structuring and chronology)
column5: Time in oral societies is measured by recurrent nature (seasons, moon), by extraordinary events (droughts, eclipses), by life spans and by social events (markets, initiations); beyond structural time no measurement exists, only an era of origins. Use in the chronology lessons: say which kind of reckoning a source uses before dating it.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 6, Structuring and chronology)
column5: Memory imposes epochs: in kingdoms everything is placed in 'the reign of' a ruler, so ruler's names attract inventions (a king said to have introduced maize); epochs restructure the record. Use in the king-list and chronology lessons: a reign-based date may be a memory device, not a count.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 3 (Vansina ch. 6, Structuring and chronology)
column5: Creation and historic time may coexist as two durations, not successive eras, among the Lugbara and Trobrianders. Use in the chronology lesson on how a society divides time.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Anachronisms in oral accounts: memory places events by a supposed migration line rather than by date (the Mbundu), transposes a horse from the eighteenth century into creation (Assiniboine), and can make events younger as well as older (Delivre's descending anachronisms). Use in the chronology lesson: check events for anachronism before using a sequence.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Test a sequence for consistency, since an inconsistent sequence shows anachronism, but a consistent one may still be a selection pattern: a Merina king cannot introduce the poison oracle if a later king is said to have done so. Use in the chronology lesson on checking king lists.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Lists and genealogies are the only chronology most oral cultures keep, and the Hopi eyewitness said it was not well to count the years. Use in the chronology lesson: oral dates are relative unless tied to outside records.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Age-grade lists can give a chronology of about a century and a half when initiations recur at regular intervals of about eight years, and a single date from writing anchors them. Use in the chronology lesson as the best case of an oral list.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Regnal lists are reliable only where each name links to the next, and versions show transposition and elision; Henige documents lengthening and shortening, so a list can give relative order but not absolute dates. Use in the king-list lessons: give the order, not the years.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Henige on generation averages: an average reign of 24.4 years in France (987 to 1793) fits no single king, so averages cannot date a particular generation; the best practice is to allot three or four generations to a century and date by vague but precise phrases. Use in the chronology lesson on averages.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Synchronisms between people who met cannot date reigns: Victoria's contemporaries William II and Napoleon III reigned at times 1837 and 1918 apart, so a synchronism between two rulers may confuse dates far apart. Use in the chronology lesson on synchronisms.

column4: ch-010.txt chunk 4 (Vansina ch. 6, Anachronism and dating)
column5: Conclusion on chronology: oral traditions give only a relative chronology except for the last century or so; date them by written sources, archaeology and astronomical or geological means. Use as the closing rule of the chronology lesson in the dates section.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Site and tradition: the Luba and Songye claim an origin at Lake Kisale, where Sanga cemeteries from the eighth century show Luba people; that dates the tradition but does not prove all Luba came from there, and southern Sudanese Funj and Luel site labels came from tradition itself (a Pope Joan case). Use in the Congo basin lesson on Sanga: a site can date a tradition without confirming it.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Independent confirmation is rare but real: a Ethiopian chronicle names Barno, and Hadiya oral accounts place him generations earlier with the same kin, confirming a single man; the Benin royal list has almost no overlap with written records before 1880. Use in the oral lesson: test overlap case by case.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: A volcanic ash in the New Guinea Highlands, dated between 1640 and 1820, shows only that events 180 to 340 years old were remembered, since no relative chronology begins before the eruption; birds and plants in the story belong to origin tales. Use in the oral lesson: a dated event proves memory depth, not a date.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Halley's comet of 1835 and an eclipse of 1680 are remembered in Kuba traditions and can be checked; astronomical links must be described well and identified by which recurrence is meant. Use in the Congo basin lesson on astronomical checks.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Linguistic checks on migration claims: the claim that Gabon's peoples all arrived after the thirteenth century cannot be right, since Bantu languages there are older; the Kololo's arrival about 1840 is borne out by the Lozi language, which relates to Sotho. Use in the Zambia and Congo basin lessons on immigration stories tested by language.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Selectivity and interpretation: traditions keep what matters to the present and reinterpret it, which leaves a cultural profile; Beidelman's denial of all evidential value goes too far, since retained information still comes from the past. Use in the oral lesson on the limits of tradition.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Messages versus artifacts: a tradition is a message with double subjectivity (sender and receiver), while a pot is direct testimony; oral traditions accumulate encoding and decoding interpretations along a chain, whereas a written source is fixed at the time of writing. Use as the core idea of the oral lesson on why oral sources need more care.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Kuba history was rewritten: a 1963 account followed the sources closely, a 1978 version used systematic linguistic comparison and economic and administrative evidence; the lesson is that outside sources correct bias and that the historian's interpretation carries more weight. Use in the Congo basin lesson on how a Kuba history was built.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 1 (Vansina ch. 7, Limitations)
column5: Degrees of limitation: recent tradition (a few generations) is rich and little distorted; origin traditions are most affected; propose the reconstruction for the last century first and go backwards. Use in the oral lesson on method.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 7, Assessment)
column5: Oral traditions are hypotheses, and the first hypothesis a modern scholar must test; a historian must justify an interpretation against the local one, not assert that a king was a culture hero or that genealogies were telescoped without reasons for each case. Use as the rule for every oral-tradition claim in the course.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 7, Assessment)
column5: Inside information: oral traditions are irreplaceable because they show populations as they saw themselves, where foreign writings say little (Benin, and the Hadiya through their own oral sources, not the Ethiopian texts). Use in the oral lesson on why oral sources are used at all.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 7, Assessment)
column5: Historians of their own past are outsiders beyond living memory; labels such as Kuba bureaucracy or Rwandan feudalism are anachronistic unless the culture's own terms support them. Use in the Great Lakes and Congo basin lessons on terms such as 'feudal' and 'bureaucracy'.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 7, Assessment)
column5: Packard: in nineteenth-century Bashu states, droughts weakened kings because kings were thought to be rainmakers, so authority withered with the crops. Use in the Congo basin lesson on kingship and rain.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 7, Assessment)
column5: Where writing fails tradition must carry reconstruction, which is slower and less reliable; field researchers should deposit recordings and the data needed to evaluate them, and oral traditions set the questions research pursues. Use as the closing rule of the oral lesson and in the sources note of the course.

column4: ch-011.txt chunk 2 (Vansina ch. 7, Assessment)
column5: Delivre reinterpreted F. Callet's older Malagasy corpus only after gaining the linguistic, cultural and social information needed to evaluate it. Use in the Madagascar lesson on Callet's material.
